title: Impossibility of Distribution-Free Predictive Inference for Individual Treatment Effects
claim: The point where two score distributions cross shifts widely with the data-generating setting, so any single validity threshold can approach zero.
layout: 6 panels in a 2x3 grid, shared legend, labeled intersection callouts
description: A 2x3 grid of line plots under the title 'CDF of |ITE − τ(X)| Under Varying Constant Propensity Scores'. Each panel is one propensity value, e(x) = 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.95, 0.975 and 0.99. The x-axis is |ITE − τ(X)| and the y-axis is the empirical CDF. Each panel has a family of blue curves, light to dark, for correlation ρ from −1.0 to 0.8. A thick red curve marks the DR pseudo score. Dots mark where the red curve crosses the blue curves. Boxed callouts with thin leader lines give the crossing heights, for example 'rho=−1.0, y=0.062'. The crossing heights range from about 0.06 to 0.99. The eye goes first to the red curve against the blue fan. A shared legend sits at the bottom.
caption: CDFs of the DR pseudo score and the true score in a simple setting with known regression functions and known constant propensity scores. The intersections vary substantially across distributions, and the effective validity threshold \(\alpha^\ast\) can be arbitrarily close to \(0\).
abstract: Uncertainty quantification for individual treatment effects (ITEs) is a daunting challenge in causal inference. Motivated by recent advances in conformal prediction, several works aim to construct distribution-free prediction sets for ITEs with desired coverage under standard assumptions such as strong ignorability and overlap. In this paper, we show that such goals are fundamentally unattainable. Specifically, we establish finite-sample and asymptotic impossibility results demonstrating that any distribution-free prediction set achieving desired coverage for ITEs must be trivial, in the sense that it has infinite expected length. This infinite-expected-length conclusion requires no regularity assumption on the covariates and holds even in their absence. Our analysis builds on ideas from the hardness of conditional independence testing and exploits the missing-data nature of causal inference. These results provide a new perspective on existing methods, clarifying that their apparent success necessarily relies on additional structural assumptions beyond standard causal assumptions.
